title: Federal Antitrust and Interstate Commerce — United States v. NexaHealth Corp.
facts: NexaHealth Corp. is the largest pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) in the United States, controlling 42% of prescription drug pricing negotiations between pharmaceutical manufacturers and health insurers. In 2024, NexaHealth acquired MedFlow Therapeutics, a mid-size PBM with 12% market share, bringing its combined control to 54% of the PBM market. The U.S. Department of Justice filed an antitrust action under Section 7 of the Clayton Act and Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act, alleging: (1) the acquisition substantially lessens competition in the PBM market, creating a near-monopoly that enables NexaHealth to inflate drug prices passed to consumers; (2) NexaHealth has engaged in exclusionary practices by requiring pharmaceutical manufacturers to use its proprietary rebate platform as a condition of formulary placement, foreclosing competitor PBMs from accessing manufacturer rebates; (3) the merger has already resulted in a 15% average increase in prescription drug costs across 23 states, directly harming consumers through the interstate commerce chain. NexaHealth argues: (1) the PBM market definition is too narrow and should include direct manufacturer-to-insurer negotiations and new digital pharmacy platforms, which would reduce its market share to 28%; (2) the acquisition created efficiencies that benefit consumers through consolidated negotiating power; (3) the exclusionary rebate platform is a legitimate business innovation protected by intellectual property rights; (4) the DOJ's price increase data is correlative, not causative, and reflects broader pharmaceutical inflation trends. The case implicates fundamental questions about market definition in the digital pharmaceutical era, the consumer welfare standard versus the competitive process standard in modern antitrust law, and whether the DOJ has standing to pursue structural remedies (forced divestiture) versus behavioral remedies. Federal circuits are split on the appropriate standard for evaluating vertical integration in healthcare markets — the Second Circuit applies a stricter consumer harm test while the Seventh Circuit uses a broader competitive effects analysis. This circuit split makes the case a candidate for Supreme Court review.
supporting_materials: FTC market analysis showing NexaHealth's 54% post-merger PBM market share. Economic expert report documenting 15% prescription drug price increases across 23 states post-acquisition. Internal NexaHealth emails discussing 'pricing leverage' gains from the merger. MedFlow acquisition documents showing $4.2 billion purchase price. Analysis of NexaHealth's proprietary rebate platform and exclusionary contracts with 17 major pharmaceutical manufacturers. Congressional testimony from independent pharmacists describing competitive foreclosure. Comparison of drug pricing in NexaHealth-dominated markets versus competitive markets. Second Circuit opinion in US v. Anthem Inc. versus Seventh Circuit opinion in FTC v. Advocate Health Care on vertical healthcare market analysis. DOJ structural remedy precedents: AT&T divestiture (1982), Standard Oil dissolution (1911).
